title: The Guide for the Perplexed
hook: written for a student torn between philosophy and faith

segments.voice: Yesterday, the messianic age: an ordinary morning, with no war and no hunger. Your line was the world, at peace. Did you take your step, or set a day for it? Day one thousand one hundred fifty-four.

A student packs his bags and leaves his teacher. He's bright, he loves the Torah, and he's been studying logic and astronomy and philosophy. And the two are pulling him apart. The verses say God walks in a garden, sits on a throne, smells the smoke of an offering. His philosophy says God can't have a body. Does he give up the books, or give up the reasoning? His teacher, far away now, decides to write for him and send the chapters as they're finished. Those chapters became a book. Today's word is its name.
screen: `A STUDENT LEAVES.` → `TORAH AND PHILOSOPHY PULL APART.` → `HIS TEACHER WRITES.`

segments.voice: Moreh Nevukhim. The Guide for the Perplexed, by Maimonides. Turn it four ways. First, the student. The book opens with a letter to a student named Joseph. Maimonides writes that Joseph came to study with him, that he was quick and eager, and that when they were separated he decided to write for him. Sometimes a book begins as one person worrying about another. Second, the reader he wants. In his introduction, Maimonides says plainly who the Guide is for. Not beginners. Not the general public. It is for a religious person, faithful and observant, who has also studied philosophy and now finds the plain sense of certain verses troubling. That person, he says, is left perplexed: follow reason and seem to abandon the Torah, or hold the Torah and feel reason has been thrown away. The book is meant to show a road that keeps both. Third, the method. Much of the opening part goes word by word through terms the Bible uses for God, words like place, standing, seeing, coming down, and shows how each can carry a figurative meaning. Fourth, the warning. Maimonides says he wrote some parts on purpose so that not everything is laid out on the surface. A reader has to work, compare chapters, and pay attention. He even asks readers not to explain the book to others hastily. So this is not a book you skim. It's a conversation with a teacher who expects you to think. Over the next days, we'll open it one chapter at a time.
screen: `A LETTER TO A STUDENT.` · `FOR THE FAITHFUL WHO ARE TORN.` · `WORD BY WORD THROUGH SCRIPTURE.` · `NOT EVERYTHING ON THE SURFACE.` · then, large: `MOREH NEVUKHIM.`

segments.voice: Settle, and let your breathing find its own pace. Now let one thing come up that genuinely perplexes you. Something about faith, or about your life, or about the world, where two things you hold seem to pull against each other. Don't solve it. Just name it, clearly, in one sentence. Then name the two sides. This is what I hold. This is what I also hold. Let them both sit there, without choosing. Notice that the Guide was written for exactly this place. The bell holds the time.
Moreh Nevukhim. The Guide for the Perplexed: Maimonides' book for a faithful reader torn between the Torah's words and philosophy. Today's word.
Your line: for the perplexed. Today, write your one-sentence perplexity somewhere you'll see it again, and keep it with you through the coming chapters. Day one thousand one hundred fifty-four.

howItsDone: Some Jews study the Guide for the Perplexed slowly, chapter by chapter, with a teacher or a study partner, in study halls, universities and adult classes.

fork.setup: you're Joseph. the Torah says God walks in a garden and sits on a throne; your philosophy says God has no body. what does your teacher's book offer?
fork.reveal: the Guide is written for exactly this reader: faithful, and perplexed, looking for a way to hold both.

original.note: Hebrew: guide (or teacher) of the perplexed, the title the book carries in Hebrew.

trapdoor: what you thought: a book of answers for confused people.
what it means: a guide for a faithful reader torn between the Torah's words and philosophy.
what a scholar hears: the dedicatory letter to Joseph, the introduction naming its reader, and its warning that parts are written so that not all is on the surface.

notes: Dedicatory letter to Joseph (ben Judah) paraphrased: came to study, quick and eager, separated, so Maimonides wrote for him. The hook's 'chapter by chapter' and 'those letters grew into a book' follow the letter's statement that he would send chapters; please confirm.

Introduction paraphrased: the book is for a religious person who has studied philosophy and is perplexed by the literal sense of scripture; not for beginners or the general public; parts deliberately not laid out plainly; request not to explain it hastily. Please confirm.
Language of composition (Judeo-Arabic) and dates deliberately left out under the claims rule.
Hook's 'walks in a garden, sits on a throne, smells the smoke of an offering' refers to biblical anthropomorphisms (Genesis 3:8, e.g. Isaiah 6:1, Genesis 8:21), paraphrased.

Editor: swapped the hook's and fork's 'hand' and 'came down to see a tower' examples for garden, throne and offering, because tomorrow's lesson is built on the tower verse and day 1157 on the hand. 'Those letters grew into a book' changed to match the dedicatory letter (he decided to write for Joseph and send chapters as they were finished). howItsDone softened to 'some Jews'.
